introduction.text: **Before you start.** By `MS-S4` you have a record of four stages: competency levels, evidence with dates, milestone bands and the journal. That record is uneven. Some competencies were shown once, under one condition, a long time ago. Others passed at *Developing* on a milestone row, and a few rest on evidence that you and the reviews disagreed about. This course turns the record into practice. You find your two or three weakest competencies, practise them in three deliberate blocks, and decide on the evidence whether each gap is closed before the capstone.

The course is personal: the gaps come from your own record, because evidence ages and weak spots are revisited (Phase 1 §10.3). This file gives one template for the gap analysis and the practice blocks, and a short catalogue of worked gap types. New evidence for each gap goes into the record against that competency's own success row (`04-competencies/`).
`REV-5` comes first in S5, so its gap analysis steers `IND-5` and `RDV-5`. A gap in a technique the capstone must show is always a candidate:

items.text: a stock- or emulsion-based sauce;
a protein to an exact doneness;
a bread or pastry element;
a preserve;
a vegetable-led course.

introduction.text: **Revision material.** The knowledge checks of S1–S4 (about 1,360 items) are your item bank. Retake the checks of the modules that taught each gap competency. If a safety item disagrees with assessment §9, follow §9.
**The gap catalogue.** The first match in this order decides priority: a safety gap, then a capstone requirement, then the oldest evidence, then the rest.

rows: A cooling log with a missing reading, or a gate passed only after a resit
Three batches cooled and logged (a stock, a braise, cooked rice), varying the quantity
Every reading within §9, the row met, none missing; always block 1
The emulsion of `MS-S2` and `MS-S4` at *Developing*; a sauce split once
The warm emulsion three times, varying the fat, then held for service
The row met at the target level, the photo *Competent*
Roast predictions outside tolerance more than pan work
Ten roast predictions, varying the cut and the oven
Last shown more than six months ago, or a household cook not yet logged
Timed cuts against the grid, varying the vegetable; or the missing cook, planned and dated
The tolerances met again, the new date in the record
Two or more entries two bands apart (assessment §3.4)
Each session scored before the outside band is seen
Disagreements down to one band or less

introduction.text: Plan three blocks of three sessions, each block spread over about three weeks: about ten weeks of calendar time at about 1.5 hours a week, alongside `IND-5` and `RDV-5`.
**Have ready:** your record and journal; the success rows of `04-competencies/`; the S1–S4 knowledge checks; the probe; the photo corner; household tasters' cards.

note.text: **Knowledge check:** none of its own. The module's two judgment objectives (choosing the gaps, and deciding whether each is closed) are shown in the plan and decisions of `REV-5.M1.X1`. Retake the knowledge checks of the modules that taught each gap competency from the S1–S4 item bank, at the same pass rule: 80 %, with every safety item correct.

blocks.text: **Why it matters:** practice without a diagnosis goes to what you already enjoy. Reading your own record honestly, and writing what "closed" means before you start, points the last weeks before the capstone at the gaps that matter.

**You need:** your record: every competency with its level, the date and conditions of each piece of evidence, the milestone bands, and the journal entries with your band and the outside band (`ORI-1`, assessment §3.4); the gap catalogue; the success rows.
**Explanation:**
*What counts as a gap:*

items.text: a competency below its stage target;
a milestone row passed at *Developing*;
evidence older than about six months: it comes up for review, but is not taken away (Phase 1 §10.3);
a level reached under fewer conditions than its row asks for;
two or more entries with a two-band disagreement (assessment §3.4).

blocks.text: *Choosing two or three.* Use the catalogue's order: safety, capstone requirements, oldest evidence, the rest. Then prefer the competencies where practice costs least and helps most across dishes. More than three spreads the practice too thin.
*The plan, per gap:*

rows: The fat: clarified, whole, brown butter
The row met; the photo *Competent*; your band within one of the outside band

blocks.text: Write the closing rule before practice starts.
*The agreement log.* From the first session of block 1, every S5 entry has your band, then the outside band. Count the share within one band every two weeks; this is the `JD-REFL` level 5 measure.
**Practice:** None: theory only.
**Look for:**

items.text: every chosen gap points to a line in the record, not to a feeling;
the closing rule is written before practice starts.

blocks.text: **If it goes wrong:**

rows: The chosen gaps are favourite techniques
Not a competency and a level
Name the competency, its row and level
Gaps that stay open, or close by hope

blocks.text: **Safety:** a safety gap always goes first, in block 1. Where an old safety item disagrees with assessment §9, §9 wins.
**Record:** the gap analysis and the plan, ready for `REV-5.M1.X1`.

**Why it matters:** ordinary cooking repeats what you already do well. Deliberate practice repeats the weak element, with feedback and one change at a time, so a block of three sessions can move a competency that months of meals did not.

**You need:** the plan for the first gap; the lesson that taught it; its knowledge check from the item bank; ingredients as the gap needs, on household meals where possible; the probe; the photo corner; tasters' cards.
**Explanation:**
*Deliberate practice.* A narrow target, repeated with feedback, one variable at a time. It is harder than ordinary cooking, and shorter.
*The lesson revisited.* Before the first session, reread the lesson that taught the competency, with its cues and faults, and retake its knowledge check.
*Feedback at every session.* A reading, a photo or a taster's card against the success row. Write your band before you see the outside band.
*The block:*

rows: The competency as the record left it, under the plan's starting condition
The success row; the knowledge check
The weak element repeated, one variable changed
Readings or photos at each attempt
The competency under the row's condition
Your band, then the outside band; the closing rule

blocks.text: A worked safety block (`SA-TEMP`): the baseline cools a stock and logs it; the practice cools a braise and a batch of cooked rice, the quantity varied; the test cools the largest batch with every reading on time.
**Practice:**

items.text: **Baseline (90 min).** The competency as the record left it, scored against the success row; the knowledge check retaken.
**Focused practice (90 min).** The weak element repeated with one variable changed; readings or photos at each attempt.
**Test (90 min).** Under the row's condition; outside band logged; the gap judged against its closing rule.

blocks.text: **Look for:**

items.text: the baseline and the test are scored the same way, so the change shows;
your band and the outside band move closer over the block.

blocks.text: **If it goes wrong:**

rows: Your band copies the outside band

blocks.text: **Safety:** the practice uses the assessment §9 figures the lesson used. For a cooling gap: from 57 °C to 21 °C within 2 hours, and to 5 °C or below within 6 hours in total; leftovers kept at most 2 days.
**Record:** the three sessions with both bands; the knowledge-check result; the decision against the closing rule.

**Why it matters:** a gap that closed in practice can open again when attention moves on. Bringing the first gap back inside an ordinary meal, while you work on the second, shows whether the first improvement held.
**You need:** the plan for the second gap; its lesson and knowledge check; the block 1 results; ingredients for a meal that uses both competencies; tasters' cards.
**Explanation:**
*The second gap.* The same pattern as block 1, on the second competency of the plan: a baseline, focused practice with one variable, and a test under the row's condition.

*Interleaving.* The first gap comes back once in this block, inside an ordinary meal, to see whether it held. A sauce gap closed in block 1, for example, returns as the sauce of a weeknight dinner in block 2, scored the same way.
*The plan adjusted in writing.* If block 1 showed the gap was larger than planned, change the plan in writing (another block, or a lower target for now), not quietly:

rows: The emulsion held for 30 minutes only once of three

blocks.text: *The closing rule stays.* A rule written before practice is not moved to fit a result. If the result falls short, the gap stays open, and block 3 or the capstone plan deals with it.
**Practice:**

items.text: **Baseline (90 min).** The second competency as the record left it, scored; its knowledge check retaken.
**Focused practice (90 min).** The weak element with one variable changed; the first gap shown once in the same meal.
**Test (90 min).** Under the row's condition; outside band logged; judged against the closing rule.

blocks.text: **Look for:**

items.text: both gaps scored on the same day show whether the first held;
every plan change has a date and a reason.

blocks.text: **If it goes wrong:**

rows: Bring it back once in a meal
A gap closed on a moved rule
The rule changed to fit the result
Keep the rule; log the shortfall

blocks.text: **Safety:** the second gap's practice uses its own §9 figures; the interleaved meal follows the rows for every dish in it, and the first gap's readings are logged again.
**Record:** the three sessions with both bands; the first gap's interleaved result; any plan change with its date and reason.

**Why it matters:** a competency that holds only in practice will fail at the capstone. A condition not yet used shows whether it holds outside practice, and a written decision turns an open gap into a known risk with a plan.
**You need:** the results of blocks 1 and 2; the plan; ingredients for a meal for at least two people other than you; their cards; the capstone plan of `CAP-5.M1.L5`.
**Explanation:**
*The weakest remaining gap.* Chosen from the results of blocks 1 and 2, or the third competency of the plan.
*A condition not yet used* (Phase 1 §10.3): time pressure, guests, or no recipe. The new condition shows whether the competency holds outside practice, which levels 4 and 5 ask for.
*Closed or not:*

items.text: **closed:** the success row met with new evidence, and the outside band agrees within one band;
**open:** the row not met, so the gap goes into the capstone plan as a known risk, with a fallback dish and a test cook (`CAP-5.M1.L5`).

blocks.text: *The written decision.* For each gap:

rows: Fallback: a *beurre blanc* style pan sauce is replaced by a stock reduction

blocks.text: **Practice:**

items.text: **Under the new condition (90 min).** For example a timed run, or the dish without a recipe.
**For others (90 min).** The competency inside a meal for at least two people other than you, scored by their cards.
**Test and decision (90 min).** The final demonstration; the decision for every gap written; the agreement log counted.

blocks.text: **Look for:**

items.text: every gap has a decision with evidence on both sides;
an open gap has a fallback in the capstone plan.

blocks.text: **If it goes wrong:**

rows: One good result under easy conditions
Plan for it: a fallback and a test cook

blocks.text: **Safety:** a meal for others follows assessment §9 for every dish, with allergens asked in advance (`NUT-3`); a safety gap is never left open into the capstone, whose food-safety row is a gate (`CAP-5.R3`).
**Record:** the three sessions; the decision table; the agreement log count; the capstone plan entries for open gaps.

exercises.title: The gap plan and three practice blocks
exercises.description: The gap-practice plan and the three blocks, with new evidence for each gap.

blocks.text: **Task:** analyse your record honestly, close the gaps that matter before the capstone, and show that your own scoring agrees with the outside evidence. Write the gap-practice plan and run three blocks, each over about three weeks. The variable changes within each block, and block 3 adds a condition not yet used. The agreement log runs over every S5 entry from block 1 on, for at least 8 weeks.
**You need:** your record and journal; the success rows of the chosen competencies; the item bank of the S1–S4 knowledge checks; ingredients as each gap needs, on household meals where possible.
*Procedure:*

items.text: Write the gap analysis: the candidates from the record, the two or three chosen, and why.
Write the plan per gap: the success row and level, the lesson revisited, the variable, the test condition, the closing rule.
Run the three blocks; at each session, write your band, then the outside band.
Write the decision for each gap, with evidence before and after; put any open gap into the capstone plan with a fallback.
Count the agreement log every two weeks, and at the end.

blocks.text: **Show:**

items.text: **The gap evidence:** for each gap, the new evidence against its own success row, entered in the record with the date and condition.

**`JD-REFL` level 5, in part:** the gap analysis and the closing decisions; the agreement log over at least 8 weeks, with at least 90 % of entries within one band of the outside evidence. `RDV-5.M3.X1` adds the style reflection, and the capstone defence (`CAP-5.M3.L3`, scored by `CAP-5.R12`) completes the row.

blocks.text: AI review reads the analysis, the plan, the session logs and the decisions: *competent* is every gap traced to a record line, a closing rule written before practice, one variable per session, your band written before the outside band, and a decision with evidence on both sides; *not yet* is a gap chosen by preference, a moved closing rule, or an open gap without a fallback.
**Time:** 13.5 h active, over about nine weeks.
